title: Unscrew a kids' toothpaste tube, put a pea-sized 0.15 to 0.35 g dab on a child's toothbrush and screw the cap back on
instruction: Get the toothbrush ready for a 4-year-old, then leave the toothpaste capped.
context: Parents put toothpaste on a young child's brush twice a day, and nearly everyone has done it: hold the tube, unscrew the cap, squeeze, screw the cap back on. For ages 3 to 6 the CDC, ADA and AAP advise no more than a pea-sized amount (about 0.25 g), yet in the CDC survey (MMWR 2019;68(4):87-90) only 49.2% of children aged 3 to 6 used a pea and over 38% used a half or full load. Swallowed fluoride while enamel forms causes fluorosis. The cap comes off only by turning it on its thread, more than one turn of the wrist, and must go back on straight and all the way. The dose is set by how far and how long the tube's walls are pressed, and the paste keeps coming briefly after the squeeze eases, so too much is the easy failure.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the counter (table) top at z 0. Toothbrush: a child's manual toothbrush (Colgate Kids Extra Soft), modeled 15.1 cm long and 14 g: a 95 x 16 x 12 mm handle, a 30 mm neck and a 26 x 12 mm head with a 20 x 9 mm bristle field 9 mm tall. It lies on its back, bristles up, along x with the head away from the robot, the bristle field's top middle at (30.0, 2.0, 1.4). Toothpaste: a Kid's Crest Cavity Protection Bubblegum 4.2 oz (119 g) tube (Target TCIN 1001365458; its directions: twist off cap), partly used: 60 g of paste left (1.30 g/mL), rolled flat from the crimp up to the paste. A round laminate body 36 mm across and 10 cm long, the rolled end 50 mm wide, a 15 mm neck with a 1.5 mm-pitch thread, and a polypropylene screw cap 35 mm across and 20.8 mm tall, 4.4 g (checked on the trial tube and cap before the first trial). The capped tube lies on its side on the counter along x, the cap toward the robot, its body's middle at (30.0, 11.0) (the front of its round body, by the shoulder, at x 25.0), the rolled end flat on the counter. Both arms start at their ready pose. What is simulated, and how, is in README.md.
scoring: Paste is scored in grams: the real trial weighs it, and the simulation converts mL at 1.30 g/mL. The trial scores 1.0 when 0.15 to 0.35 g is on the bristle field (a pea-sized dab: the CDC pea is 0.25 g), at most 0.05 g is anywhere else, the cap is screwed fully on, the bristles face within 45 degrees of up, the tube and the brush both rest on the counter (lowest point within 3 mm of it) with no part of either arm touching them or the cap (in simulation every arm link at least 5 mm clear), each was let go resting on the counter (lowest point within 5 mm, moving under 0.3 m/s), not dropped or thrown, and all is still (under 1 cm/s) for 1 s. It scores 0.75 for the same dose, clean and capped, when any other condition for 1.0 is not met (for example not yet let go, dropped or thrown, or not yet still). A tube left uncapped, or its cap not screwed fully on, caps the score at 0.5. It scores 0.5 for a pea-sized dab with more than 0.05 g off the bristles, and 0.25 for 0.05 to 0.15 g (a smear, the under-3 dose) or 0.35 to 0.70 g (too much, a half load). Turning the bristles past sideways with paste on them caps the score at 0.25. Otherwise it scores 0, including under 0.05 g and over 0.70 g. Doing nothing scores 0 (the tube starts capped, with no paste out). Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. Screwed fully on: the cap turned down to within 45 degrees of its seat, square and centered; in simulation read from the cap's own pose on the neck: its turn within 45 degrees of the seated turn, on the thread's last turn (within half the 1.5 mm pitch of its seat), its axis within 2 degrees and 0.6 mm of the neck's; in a real trial a tester turns the cap clockwise by hand after the trial and it stops within an eighth of a turn and sits square, with an even gap between the cap's mouth and the shoulder all round. Paste leaves only an uncapped nozzle, and lands on the bristles only from a nozzle pointing within 60 degrees of down and at most 3 cm above them, while they face within 60 degrees of up; otherwise it lands off them. Touching is contact of an arm's own collision hulls, within 1 mm. Real trial (AWS-100-CAL 0.01 g scale): weigh the brush and the tube with its cap before; after, photograph the head from above beside a steel rule, wipe any paste off the brush outside the bristle field and weigh the brush (on the bristles = its gain); weigh the tube with its cap unwiped (dispensed = its loss); off the bristles = dispensed minus on the bristles. Cap check by hand as above; bristle angle, arms off the tube, cap and brush, and the let-go from the video.
reset_notes: Room at 20-24 C (the paste's stiffness changes with temperature). Each trial uses a clean, dry brush (weighed) laid at its mark, and the tube with 50 to 70 g of paste left (gross weight minus the weighed empty tube and cap): roll it flat from the crimp up to the paste, hold it nozzle up and press gently until paste fills the nozzle to its mouth, wipe the nozzle flush, screw the cap on with the fingertips until it just stops (no extra twist), lay the tube at its mark and let it rest 1 min so the laminate springs back. In simulation the tube always holds 60 g, starts capped, and the brush starts clean.
fidelity: Rigid bodies. The cap is a free body on its thread: the neck's and the cap's ridges are helices of convex hulls with the ISO metric 60-degree section, so it comes off and goes on only by turning, about 1.1 turns. The tube's body is a rigid core with four sprung wall panels. The paste is a flow model, not a fluid: pressure from the panels' push on trapped air, a yield pressure, flow past it, dropped plumb from an uncapped nozzle onto a 1 mm bristle grid (README).
